props.title: Two or Three Things I Know About Her
props.initialSlug: A woman's double life mirrors 60s Paris in flux

sections.content: Jean-Luc Godard's Two or Three Things I Know About Her (1967) marks a crucial turning point in French New Wave cinema, where the movement's playful experimentation evolved into more pointed political commentary. The film follows Juliette Jeanson, a middle-class housewife who turns to prostitution to maintain her consumerist lifestyle. Godard's whispered narration and direct camera addresses shatter conventional narrative, while his obsessive focus on construction sites and commercial spaces in Paris creates a damning portrait of modern capitalism. This technique influenced later works like Jeanne Dielman, 23 Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975) and Safe (1995) in their clinical examination of women's domestic spaces.

sections.content: The film's innovative sound design, mixing whispered philosophical commentary with diegetic city noise, established new possibilities for cinema's political voice. This approach directly influenced later essay films like Sans Soleil (1983) and News From Home (1977). Godard's technique of interrupting narrative with documentary footage of Vietnam War protests and construction sites created a template for how cinema could weave political critique into its formal structure.

Marina Vlady's performance as Juliette pioneered a new kind of anti-naturalistic acting that would influence European art cinema for decades. Her direct addresses to camera and matter-of-fact descriptions of prostitution created a Brechtian distance that later directors like Chantal Akerman and Michael Haneke would adopt in films like Every Man for Himself (1980) and The Piano Teacher (2001). movies.title: Masculin Féminin
movies.slug: Godard explores youth culture and consumerism in 1960s Paris

sections.content: The film's examination of consumerism and female objectification laid groundwork for feminist cinema of the 1970s. Works like Riddles of the Sphinx (1977) and Born in Flames (1983) built on Godard's techniques of fragmentation and direct address to create explicitly political works. His use of commercial imagery and brand names as symbols of cultural imperialism influenced filmmakers like Harun Farocki and Alexander Kluge in their essay films about capitalism.
